rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-record screening limits)
rules.requirement: A housing provider may not use an application that asks about criminal records, or make any oral or written inquiry about them, before a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration. At no point may it evaluate arrests or charges without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. After a conditional offer it may consider only two kinds of record. The first is convictions for murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, listed sexual offenses, or crimes requiring lifetime sex-offender registration. The second is indictable offenses within set lookbacks: 6 years for first degree, 4 years for second or third degree, and 1 year for fourth degree. An offer may be withdrawn only if the provider finds, by a preponderance of the evidence, that withdrawal is necessary to a substantial, legitimate and nondiscriminatory interest, after an individualized assessment of listed factors. The provider must give written notice of the specific reasons and an opportunity to appeal. The applicant may request, within 30 days, the information relied on, and the provider must supply it free within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. Standards must be applied in a nondiscriminatory manner. Providers may not publish advertisements excluding people with records, require drug or alcohol tests, or seek drug-treatment records. Complaints go only to the Division on Civil Rights, not to court, and the Division offers a 14-day mediation window. Penalties are up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations. The Director may also order return of the application fee.
rules.key_value: Post-offer lookback: 6 yrs (1st degree), 4 yrs (2nd/3rd degree), 1 yr (4th degree); no lookback for listed serious crimes or lifetime registration; record request within 30 days, free copy within 10 days; penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Starting January 1 of the year after enactment, the cap is adjusted each year by the CPI (All Urban Consumers, NY-Northern NJ-Long Island, All Items), but only if the change is greater than zero. The Director of Consumer Affairs publishes the limit. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later offense. They are enforced by summary proceedings brought by the Director or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant from the collected penalty. The Director must adopt rules, including a mechanism for reporting violations.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee (CPI adjustment begins January 1, 2027); penalties up to $500 / $750 / $1,000

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A landlord may collect a security deposit of at most 1.5 times one month's rent. Pet deposits and prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, count toward the cap. At lease inception no more than 2.5 months' rent may be required, including first month's rent. Yearly increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit is held in trust, may not be commingled, and must be kept in an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey institution. Interest belongs to the tenant. The landlord must give written notice of the institution, amount, account type and interest rate within 30 days of receipt and at each annual interest payment. If notice or interest is not given, the tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% per annum interest to rent after written notice. The deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions sent by registered or certified mail, must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Return is due within 5 business days when a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation, and within 15 business days after a Safe Housing Act termination. Wrongful withholding allows recovery of double the amount, plus costs and attorney's fees. A new owner is responsible for the deposit.
rules.key_value: Max 1.5x monthly rent (2.5x including first month at inception); annual increase max 10% of current deposit; return within 30 days; double damages for wrongful withholding

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Landlords holding deposits for ten or fewer units must use an insured New Jersey bank or savings and loan interest-bearing account. Those with 10 or more units may alternatively use an insured money market fund of a New Jersey-based investment company or a variable-rate account.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement:
A residential landlord may not evict or fail to renew a lease, written or oral, without good cause. The statutory causes are:
- nonpayment of rent
- disorderly conduct
- willful or grossly negligent damage
- substantial breach of rules or lease covenants after a Notice to Cease
- failure to pay a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with municipal ordinances
- health and safety removal or illegal occupancy
- permanent retirement from residential use
- refusal of reasonable lease changes
- habitual late payment
- condominium, cooperative or fee-simple conversion
- owner or buyer occupancy in small buildings or converted units
- end of employment-based tenancy
- certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking offenses
A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment, and some causes also require a Notice to Cease. Notice periods vary by cause. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal can remove a tenant, and self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance of six times monthly rent. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings may be evicted only for a narrower list of causes, with 3-month or 1-month notice for lease expiration. Rooming and boarding houses follow the same causes and notices, plus 3 working days' notice to the County Welfare Board. Misusing a unit after an owner-occupancy or retirement eviction exposes the landlord to treble damages, and to civil penalties of up to $10,000 for residential reuse within 5 years.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit: 3 days (disorderly, damage, employment end, criminal causes); 1 month (rule/lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, habitual late payment); 2 months (post-conversion owner/buyer occupancy); 3 months (health and safety removal); 18 months (retirement from residential use); 3 years (conversion). Relocation 6x monthly rent for illegal occupancy; treble damages and up to $10,000 civil penalty for misuse.

Notice to quit is 3 months (at-will or year-to-year), 1 month (month-to-month), or 3 days for disorderly, destructive or rule-violation causes.
coverage.other_conditions: Hotel and motel guests with no alternate residence who live there continuously are covered. Landlords who have not properly registered under the landlord identity law cannot obtain an eviction until they comply.

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections and notices (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. A buyer of a foreclosed property who wants to occupy it as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit, and a tenant whose lease runs longer cannot be evicted until it expires. Anyone acquiring a foreclosed property with rental units must notify tenants in English and Spanish within 10 business days after the sale that ownership has changed and they need not move. In buildings with more than 10 units, the notice is posted in a prominent location instead. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. A monetary offer to induce a tenant to leave must come with a separate notice, and the tenant gets a five-day review period. Pressure tactics are prohibited, including harassment and rent increases above rent control or unconscionable increases.
rules.key_value: 90-day notice to quit for buyer occupancy; tenant notice within 10 business days after sale (English and Spanish); 5-day review period for buyout offers

coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental units in foreclosed properties. Month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units are not exempt from the 90-day notice. Posting replaces individual notices in buildings with more than 10 units.
coverage.other_conditions: Triggered by foreclosure and the sale or transfer of title.

rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.

rules.review_note: The guide grounds the 90-day notice in Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson and cites no specific statute for it. The citation reflects the Foreclosure Fairness Act sections named for the notice duties.

rules.title: Reprisal (anti-retaliation) protections for tenants
rules.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant through eviction, substantial alteration of the lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease because the tenant exercised protected rights. Protected rights are: enforcing lease or legal rights; a good-faith complaint to a governmental authority after written notice to the landlord and reasonable time to correct; organizing or joining a lawful tenant organization; and refusing lease changes made in retaliation. A tenant may sue for damages.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (conversion protections)
rules.requirement: Qualifying tenants in a building being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership may obtain protected tenancy status. Qualifying tenants are those aged 62 or older before the conversion recording date, permanently disabled tenants, and honorably discharged veterans with a service-connected disability of 60% or more. They must have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date. Protected tenants may be shielded from eviction for 40 years if family income is not more than three times the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of their right to apply, and applications are generally due within 60 days. Separately, under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31, rents in a converted building may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. This applies to all tenants in the building, whether or not they are protected. Increases for new services or amenities remain allowed.
rules.key_value: Eviction protection for up to 40 years; income limit 3x county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater; applications generally within 60 days; no rent increase to recover conversion-only costs (all tenants)

coverage.other_conditions: Tenant must have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date. Triggered by a conversion.

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics in rental
rules.requirement: The LAD bars housing discrimination based on source of lawful income or source of lawful rent payment, among other protected characteristics. These include race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital, civil union or domestic partnership status, familial status, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability and nationality. A landlord cannot deny a Section 8 HUD voucher holder the right to rent based solely on that source of income. Discriminatory advertising is prohibited. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income, an oversized family, a zoning-violating occupancy, or poor credit history. Complaints may be filed free with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or in Superior Court within two years. Fines can reach $10,000 for a first offense.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement:
Each of the following is unlawful and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act:
- a rental property owner or its agent paying for, subscribing to or contracting for the services of a coordinator
- a coordinator facilitating an agreement among owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function
- any person engaging in or facilitating parallel pricing coordination
- any person performing a coordinating function
A coordinating function is algorithmic or automated rent-setting, or recommendation of rents, lease terms or occupancy levels, that uses nonpublic competitively sensitive information of other owners or applies a common algorithm for two or more owners. Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 through 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact ordinances that conflict with the act.
rules.key_value: Violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; effective on the first day of the twelfth month after the July 20, 2026 enactment (July 1, 2027); conflicting municipal ordinances barred

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Applies to any rental property owner owning one or more rental residential dwelling units. Controlled entities count as a single owner.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units in New Jersey (houses, apartments, accessory units and other primary residences). It excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
coverage.other_conditions: Not a coordinating function: research, statistical or testing use not used to set terms; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend rents; government affordability controls. Not an algorithmic device: non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data.

rules.exemptions: Research, statistical or testing uses; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage databases; government affordability controls; non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis; query-only databases. Inpatient medical, long-term care and correctional facilities are not residential dwelling units.

rules.conflict_note: Possible preemption between levels. Section 6(b) bars municipalities from enacting ordinances that conflict with the act. Jersey City (Jersey City Code § 218-12, Ord. 25-057 as amended by Ord. 25-076) and Hoboken (Hoboken City Code § 158-2) already have algorithmic rent-fixing ordinances in force. It is unresolved whether those ordinances conflict, whether 6(b) reaches ordinances already enacted, and whether they survive once the act takes effect on July 1, 2027.
rules.review_note: Section 6(b) does not name specific cities. The act creates no standalone penalty schedule; enforcement runs through the Antitrust Act remedies.

The FAIR Act takes effect on July 1, 2027, providing affected property owners, managers, and software providers time to review and, if necessary, modify their pricing practices before the law becomes effective.

The FAIR Act prohibits residential rental property owners from using algorithmic revenue management software that collects or processes competitors' nonpublic leasing information to set or recommend rental prices.
